newsitem.title: UK: British utilities slip as Labour heads for power.
newsitem.headline: British utilities slip as Labour heads for power.

text.p: Politically sensitive UK utilities stocks were marked down slightly in thin after-hours trade on Friday after TV exit polls predicted a resounding victory for the opposition Labour party in the British election.
Dealers estimated the effect of the sector's markdown would be to take 15-20 points off the FTSE 100 index of leading shares.
The FTSE finished up 9 points at 4,445.0 on Thursday.
"The market will find it very difficult to push ahead if the polls are upheld," said one dealer. "People will certainly be re-appraising utilities."

Labour has pledged a windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities. In the months ahead of the election, the sector has been weighed down by speculation over the possible size and extent of the tax.
Early results from the ballot, which have pointed to a landslide, have generated market worries that Labour's plans may be unchecked.
"People have to accept that we are looking at a big Labour victory here and things are not going to be as quiet tommorrow as they have been for the last six weeks," said an equity salesman.

In a thinly populated market dealers reported a few "enquiries" but little interest in trading as results began to emerge. The first Conservative seat to fall showed a 10 percent swing to Labour. Labour needs only a 4.3 percent swing nationwide to gain power, but opinion polls had been predicting a landslide for some time.
"The result is turning out as predicted and at the moment there isn't an awful lot of demand for dealing," one trader said. "It's early days...but we have had enquiries in the utilities area."

Sharelink, Europe's largest execution stockbroker, said business had been split 55:45 on the sell side since the market's official close. The most popular buy was British Telecom while Abbey National topped the sell list.
City bookmaker IG index cut the FTSE opening price spread to 4,432-4,440 by 2344 GMT. IG said the volume of business "is nothing like the last election, it's very quiet."
"People are being very wary about the size of the Labour majority, judging by the slowness of the market reaction compared with daylight hours," the equity salesman said.
